message.content: Reality is a small warm point in a sea of color and shape. In a world made of floating arcs, dripping blues, and torn swaths of gold, there was only one creature that could be touched: a hedgehog named Pip. His spines were real, his breath was real, and his round glasses, held together by a tiny brass screw, were real too. The world around him did not look like a place to live; it looked like a painting that had forgotten how to finish. The abstract world does not obey fixed form, so Pip must learn to move by feeling rather than sight. He walked across a field of violet triangles that softened under his feet like wet paper. A river of thick red paint ran sideways through the air, and Pip leapt over it without thinking. Sometimes the ground became a spiral, sometimes a shadow stretched into a ladder, and sometimes a single black line hung in the sky like a question. Pip’s paws knew more than his eyes, so he trusted them. Other things in the world are fragments of a painting, not living beings. A bird made of blue brushstrokes flapped beside him, but it had no warmth and no weight. A cat assembled from grey smudges blinked with hollow eyes, then dissolved into a cloud of silver dots. Trees were only suggestions of trees: tall strokes of green and brown that never grew leaves. Pip missed real animals, real insects, real wind, but he kept walking because there was no one else to be sad with. Pip’s glasses do not correct his vision; they help him see the hidden logic of chaos. When he put the brass screw to his lips and whispered, “Show me,” the lenses shimmered. The wild tangle of color arranged itself for a moment: a path formed between a storm of yellow dashes, a bridge appeared where two shapes almost touched, and a door made of soft pink shadows opened in a wall of dark blue. The abstract world was not random, Pip discovered; it was only waiting to be read. Even in abstraction, a small real heart can make the whole canvas alive. Pip found a small hollow shaped like a nest among the curves and angles. He curled inside it, and for the first time the painting around him seemed to breathe. The colors brightened, the lines steadied, and the fragments of birds and cats and trees turned toward him as if listening. He was still the only real creature there, but that did not matter now. His heartbeat was the quiet rhythm that taught the abstract world how to live.
